articles.title: CEA: Year 2026 resembles 1991
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The year 2026 resembles 1991, and it could be deemed an inflection point for the Indian economy, which has been facing not only external
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The year 2026 resembles 1991, and it could be deemed an inflection point for the Indian economy, which has been facing not only external challenges but also structural constraints in manufacturing, energy, agriculture and technology, chief economic adviser V Anantha Nageswaran said on Thursday.Addressing the ISID-IDRA national conference, Nageswaran further said that, in the global context, India is a source of macroeconomic stability and resilience, which sometimes tend to get forgotten in the noisy world of social media narratives.“2026 resembles 1991, and many of you immediately should not think that when we talk about the word resemblance, it is not the same as identical. Identical means that you have the same balance of payments crisis.“No. The point is, it was an inflection point for us in 1991, and 2026 is also, or even 2025, could be deemed as inflection points for us,” he said. Nageswaran said that while the 1991 balance of payments crisis brought four decades of accumulated constraints to a head — a moment of reckoning more than a passing shock — the external stress of 2026 has brought India to a fork in its growth journey and invites a fundamental re-examination of strategy.“In 2026, the challenge is not only external. Structural constraints in manufacturing, energy, agriculture and technology add to the pressure,” he said.Nageswaran said govts and industries must focus on building domestic capabilities and reducing dependence on supplies that could be restricted during geopolitical tensions.“The 21st century will be marked by a geopolitical contest for real resources,” he said, adding that the key question was how much leverage a country could exercise to secure what it needs. Nageswaran pointed out that the worst shocks now arrive not because of accidents of nature, but by design. “Just as last week, we saw China announcing an export licensing regime for tunnel boring machines and for many other products of infrastructure goods, which India will be needing,” he said.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Crude oil prices continued their upward march on Friday, with Brent crossing $115 a barrel as attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and mounting risks to
articles.body: Crude oil prices continued their upward march on Friday, with Brent crossing $115 a barrel as attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and mounting risks to shipping in the Gulf heightened fears of supply disruptions. The benchmarks were also heading for their fourth consecutive monthly rise, with US crude poised to settle above $100 for the first time since April.Brent futures gained 86 cents, or 0.75 per cent, to $115.74 a barrel by 0122 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) rose 72 cents, or 0.71 per cent, to $102.72.Brent was on course for a nearly 14 per cent gain in October, while WTI was set to jump around 15 per cent. Both were heading for their sharpest monthly increases since July.The latest escalation came on Thursday, when Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi group claimed attacks on key Saudi oil installations, including the Ras Tanura and Rabigh refineries and an Aramco facility in Abqaiq. A Saudi-led coalition separately reported intercepting a cruise missile launched towards the kingdom’s western region.The developments have heightened concerns over the security of energy infrastructure and shipping routes at a time when prospects for a diplomatic breakthrough remain uncertain.“Continued kinetic action around the Strait of Hormuz amidst doubts of a viable diplomatic pathway are keeping oil prices elevated in expectation of an escalation of the conflict in coming weeks,” said Saul Kavonic, head of energy research at MST Marquee.The Strait of Hormuz remains a major source of concern for energy markets, with any disruption to traffic through the waterway threatening to constrain global oil supplies.Peace overtures fail to ease tensionsEfforts to reopen diplomatic channels between Washington and Tehran have yet to provide markets with reassurance.US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that Vice President JD Vance had contacted Iran to help it obtain medical supplies. This followed US media reports that Vance had written to Iran’s top security official in a bid to restart peace negotiations.Iran has received the letter but has not responded, the semi-official Tasnim news agency reported. Tehran is insisting that Washington accept its conditions, the agency said, quoting the Iranian position that “any position that contradicts this framework is unacceptable.”At sea, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards reported that three tankers had hit sea mines, exploded and caught fire while attempting to use an unauthorised route south of the Strait of Hormuz. The report added to the security concerns surrounding maritime traffic in the region.The heightened risks are also prompting changes to corporate travel plans. ExxonMobil and Chevron have cancelled plans for their executives to attend the United Arab Emirates’ biggest oil show next week, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters.With crude prices already recording substantial monthly gains, traders are watching for signs that the conflict could further disrupt oil production or transportation. The trajectory of diplomatic efforts and the security of key energy routes are likely to remain central to market sentiment.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: World’s largest crypto exchange hit by world’s largest heist
articles.summary: Hackers stole over $6 billion in cryptocurrency on Thursday, shattering the record for the largest such heist as multiple investigators pointed the finger at North Korea.
articles.body: Hackers stole over $6 billion in cryptocurrency on Thursday, shattering the record for the largest such heist as multiple investigators pointed the finger at North Korea. As of Thursday night in the US, a team of cryptocurrency firms had managed to freeze about $3 billion of the stolen loot amid a frenetic battle with the hackers to find and control the digital money. The hackers broke into digital wallets held at Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange. Binance said late Thursday that its initial investigation indicates that the hack went through an engineer’s laptop, “which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” Binance said it would “cover all losses” from “the company’s funds” and an emergency assets fund, adding “user funds are safe.” The crypto exchange also said it had “temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks are completed; revoked the affected address authorization; [and] engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds.” Analysts were shocked by the amount of money impacted. “It’s the biggest hack in history,” Aravind Srinivasan, head of large crypto market maker GSR’s systematic OTC business, told Reuters. Crypto-tracing firm TRM Labs attributed the heist to an elite North Korean hacking unit, “based on robust on and off-chain intelligence.” Pangolin Intelligence, another blockchain-tracking firm based in Singapore, said it also believed that a North Korean hacking unit was behind the heist. “Analyzing the on-chain activity related to this hack and correlating with information gathered from previous known incidents [involving the North Korean cyber unit]” led to the attribution, said an analyst with Pangolin Intelligence, who did not want to be named for privacy reasons. “I think the cat and mouse game has barely begun yet,” the Pangolin Intelligence analyst told CNN, adding that North Korea was likely poised to tap a network of money laundering organizations to try to cash out the stolen funds. Chainalysis, another crypto-tracking company, said it was monitoring stolen funds “moving across multiple blockchains,” including Bitcoin and Ethereum. A Chainalysis spokesperson told CNN the firm had “high confidence” North Korea was behind the hack. CNN has reached out to North Korea’s mission at the UN for comment. Pyongyang has previously denied hacking allegations. CNN has requested comment from the FBI, as well as the US Secret Service, which also investigates cybercrime. In past investigations of big crypto hacks, the FBI has had an on-call team of analysts that worked to freeze some of the money. If North Korea is proven to be the culprit, it would be little surprise to US law enforcement officials and private experts. North Korean hackers were blamed for the previous record-high crypto hack, when they allegedly stole $1.5 billion from Bybit, another major cryptocurrency exchange. In that case, the attackers stole an amount equal to a significant portion of North Korea’s reported annual gross domestic product in a matter of minutes. North Korea’s formidable hacking teams are a key source of revenue for the nuclear-armed, sanctions-battered regime, according to current and former US and South Korean officials. Pyongyang-linked hackers have stolen billions of dollars from banks and cryptocurrency firms in the last several years, according to reports from the United Nations and private firms. A 2023 CNN investigation spotlighted how the South Korean intelligence service worked with private crypto-tracking experts to seize about $1 million in cryptocurrency that North Koreans had stolen from a victim. Unlike platforms for trading stocks, cryptocurrency exchanges tend to hold digital assets on their users’ behalf, which make them more vulnerable to hackers and theft, particularly given a lack of regulatory oversight within the relatively nascent industry. Binance was co-founded in 2017 by Canadian national Changpeng Zhao, becoming the world’s largest crypto trading platform within a year of its launch. However, Zhao stepped down in 2023 after pleading guilty to violating anti-money laundering laws in the US. He was sentenced to four months in federal prison, and was pardoned by President Donald Trump in October last year. Zhao, who no longer manages the platform but remains its largest shareholder, said on X that the incident appeared to be a hack and that he expects user funds to be fully covered by the exchange. Prices of Bitcoin and Ether, the most widely-traded cryptocurrencies, plummeted following news of the Binance breach, but regained some losses to trade about 2-3% lower midday Friday in Hong Kong. The is a breaking news story, more to come.

articles.title: Google parent Alphabet loses $500 billion in market value as AI spending spooks investors
articles.summary: Shares of Google parent Alphabet plunged more than 12% on Thursday, wiping out around $500 billion in market value in one of the biggest single-day losses
articles.body: Shares of Google parent Alphabet plunged more than 12% on Thursday, wiping out around $500 billion in market value in one of the biggest single-day losses in stock market history. The sell-off reflected growing investor concerns over the company's escalating artificial intelligence spending, slowing growth in its search advertising business and uncertainty over how quickly its investments will generate returns.The decline marked Alphabet's worst single-day fall on record, exceeding its losses during the Covid-19 pandemic and the 2008 financial crisis, according to CNN. The market value erosion was the second-largest single-day loss recorded by a company, after chipmaker Nvidia lost nearly $600 billion in early 2025.The sharp fall followed Alphabet's quarterly earnings report, released on Wednesday, which showed sales below analysts' expectations. Investors were particularly concerned about the outlook for Google's search advertising business, which has long been a major source of revenue and profit.The company is facing growing competition from artificial intelligence-powered chatbots that allow users to seek information without relying on traditional search results. Investors fear this shift could weaken Google's advertising business if consumers increasingly turn to AI tools, including those developed by competitors, to find answers online.The concern is that the transition could happen faster than Google can adapt its business model. Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management, told CNN that the displacement of traditional search could happen “faster than Google can react to it and pivot their business.”AI spending raises questions about returnsAlongside concerns about its core search business, Alphabet's rapidly rising expenditure on AI infrastructure has intensified scrutiny of its financial performance.The company reported $51.4 billion in capital expenditure in the third quarter alone, compared with $91.4 billion for the whole of 2025. The spending includes investments in data centres and computing infrastructure needed to develop and operate AI services.While technology companies are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into infrastructure to compete in the AI race, investors are increasingly questioning whether the spending will translate into sustainable profits.A key concern for Alphabet is its free cash flow, which measures the cash remaining after operating expenses and capital investments. The company recorded negative free cash flow for a second consecutive quarter, according to CNN. Before this year, Google had not reported a negative figure for any quarter since going public in 2004.Negative free cash flow does not necessarily indicate that a company is unprofitable. However, it means less cash is available after investment spending to fund shareholder returns, including dividends and share buybacks, or to support other business priorities.Alphabet's performance stood in contrast to Microsoft, which reported $18.6 billion in free cash flow for the third quarter despite continuing to invest heavily in AI infrastructure. Microsoft's shares ended Thursday's session largely unchanged, while Alphabet suffered a double-digit decline.“We are now getting to see who is spending rationally on AI and who is not,” Richard Reyle, chief investment officer at Questar Capital Partners, told CNN.Why investors are becoming cautious about AIThe sell-off highlights a broader shift in how markets are evaluating the AI boom. Investors are no longer looking only at the scale of companies' investments or the growth potential of the technology. They are also assessing whether those investments can generate adequate returns, how much cash they consume and whether AI could undermine existing revenue streams.Alphabet is attempting to expand its AI capabilities while defending its dominant search business. Its investments could help it compete in a rapidly changing technology market, but the returns remain uncertain as the industry races to build data centres and secure computing capacity.Even the prospect of future demand from AI companies does not guarantee immediate profitability. Although AI firms are committing to large amounts of computing power, the financial benefits depend on whether demand continues to grow and whether the infrastructure can be monetised at a sufficient scale.Technology companies are also increasingly turning to debt and financial markets to fund their ambitions, raising questions about the sustainability of the industry's capital spending.“Everybody is trying to get through the door at the same time, and it gives people pause,” Ted Mortonson, a technology-focused investment strategist at Baird, told CNN.For Alphabet, the challenge is to demonstrate that its massive AI investments can produce profitable growth without weakening the cash-generating search business that has supported the company for years. Thursday's steep decline suggests investors are demanding clearer evidence of those returns rather than accepting spending growth as a sign of future success.You use AI every day. articles.title: Why isn’t China’s AI and tech boom saving its stock markets?
articles.summary: The global artificial intelligence boom that has helped sustain Chinese economic momentum this year still can’t offset its domestic woes, particularly in its stock market.
articles.body: The global artificial intelligence boom that has helped sustain Chinese economic momentum this year still can’t offset its domestic woes, particularly in its stock market. Since peaking in June, key Chinese indexes have fallen more than 20%, crossing the threshold for a bear market. Beijing responded last week by pumping $19 billion into exchange-traded funds, according to Bloomberg data, its biggest intervention since early 2025, when US President Donald Trump’s tariff offensive roiled global markets. But analysts say interventions like this may do little to arrest the persistent slide, amid weak consumer spending and concerns over a possible bursting of the AI bubble. On Thursday, China’s benchmark CSI 300 index of stocks listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen closed down 1%. Even national tech champions that have helped fuel a record trade surplus this year could not escape the crash. Shanghai’s STAR50 index, composed of China’s homegrown AI and chip leaders, has plunged more than 40% since a June peak. Meanwhile, shares in the world’s largest humanoid robot maker by sales Unitree, which surged 600% in its Shanghai debut in August, have halved, and the valuation of memory chipmaker CXMT, which became Shanghai’s top weighted stock three months after listing, has fallen by nearly 30% since its August peak. “The selloff reflects a repricing of crowded AI trades, weak domestic demand, and the lack of stimulus,” said Gary Ng, senior economist for Asia Pacific at Natixis Corporate and Investment Bank. The meltdown of stocks also extended to Hong Kong, where the benchmark Hang Seng index has plummeted more than 12% this year. Together with Indonesia and India, stocks in China have emerged as the worst performers in the region this year. Ng explained that Hong Kong faces pressure through its exposure to Chinese companies and selling by mainland investors. Beijing’s increasing scrutiny of cross-border investments and tightening of offshore tax rules also contributed to the plunge, he said. “Any measure to address the stock market sentiment tends to be short-lived if there are no policies to address underlying key issues,” said Lorraine Tan, director of equity research in Asia at Morningstar, a financial services firm. “There are imbalances in China’s economy, including excess capacity in many sectors, that need to be addressed. The lack of fiscal spending this year has also been a drag,” she said, adding that measures are needed to boost domestic consumption. China’s stock rout offers a cautionary tale as investors and analysts warn that an abrupt collapse of the debt-fueled AI boom could send tech stocks, which have soared this year, tumbling worldwide. For now, China’s equity sell-off is unlikely to trigger significant spillovers into global markets, experts said. Strict controls on capital flows limit foreign investors’ participation in Chinese markets, reducing the possibility that turmoil could spread internationally. Still, within China, the selloff is hitting some retail investors at one of the worst possible times. While demand for AI chips and hardware worldwide has accelerated Chinese exports this year and lifted the country to expectation-beating third-quarter growth, stagnant domestic consumption and a prolonged housing market downturn continue to drag. About 70% of Chinese household wealth is tied up in property. But since the sector began unravelling five years ago, household savings have remained trapped in falling assets, driving some capital into the domestic stock market. However, with Beijing tightening restrictions on offshore trading to curb capital flight in recent months, mainland retail investors face increasingly limited options. “Chinese equities have generally underperformed most markets this year, and this could contribute to a negative wealth effect that further softens household confidence,” said Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at Dutch bank ING. At a financial forum in Beijing last week, Wu Qing, chairman of the country’s market regulator, vowed to prioritize stability and “do everything possible to maintain the safety and stability of the capital market.” “We will also encourage eligible listed companies to step up share buybacks and increase their holdings of their own shares, delivering better returns to investors,” he added.

articles.title: Amazon shares sink 7% as AI spending fuels cash-burn concerns, overshadow cloud growth
articles.summary: Amazon shares fell sharply in after-hours trading on Thursday (local time) as heavy artificial intelligence investments and a weaker-than-expected
articles.body: Amazon shares fell sharply in after-hours trading on Thursday (local time) as heavy artificial intelligence investments and a weaker-than-expected earnings performance overshadowed accelerating growth in its cloud computing business.The e-commerce and technology giant’s shares dropped as much as 7% after it reported third-quarter results that missed Wall Street expectations and issued a cautious revenue outlook for the crucial holiday shopping quarter. The stock had already fallen 4.3% during regular trading to close at $243.79.Amazon’s cloud computing unit, Amazon Web Services (AWS), delivered a standout performance, with revenue rising 39% year-on-year to $46 billion in the quarter ended September 30. This marked its fastest growth in nearly five years and accelerated from the 37% increase recorded in the previous quarter. Revenue also exceeded analysts’ expectations of $45.61 billion, according to LSEG data.However, investors remained concerned about the cost of expanding the business to capitalise on growing demand for artificial intelligence. Amazon has forecast capital expenditure of $220 billion for 2026, largely to build AI data centres and expand its technology infrastructure.Chief executive Andy Jassy told analysts that capital expenditure would be “meaningfully more” next year, without providing a specific figure. “Our strategy is working and I expect it will for the foreseeable future,” Jassy said, defending the company’s investment plans.He also said AWS could become a business generating more than $1 trillion in annual revenue within five to 10 years, adding that demand for the unit’s services remained strong.“Customers are gobbling it up,” Jassy said, referring to the rapid adoption of Amazon’s AI infrastructure.Cash burn and outlook weigh on sentimentAmazon’s spending plans have raised questions about how quickly its AI investments will translate into stronger cash generation. The company reported a trailing 12-month cash burn of $42.4 billion in the September quarter, driven by heavy capital expenditure. Spending on capital projects during the quarter reached $77.26 billion, around $20 billion above estimates compiled by LSEG.“The free cash flow looks like the ugly part of the report,” said Dave Wagner, portfolio manager at Aptus Capital Advisors. “Operations generated plenty of cash but their capex just absolutely swallowed it.”Amazon reported net sales of $201.94 billion for the quarter, up 12% from $180.17 billion a year earlier. Net income declined to $20.69 billion, or $1.89 per share, from $21.19 billion, or $1.95 per share, in the year-ago period. Analysts had expected earnings of $1.97 per share on revenue of $202.2 billion, according to FactSet.The company forecast fourth-quarter net sales of between $240 billion and $247 billion, representing growth of 12% to 16% from a year earlier. The midpoint of the range, $243.5 billion, was slightly below analysts’ estimate of $244.51 billion, according to LSEG.The outlook covers the holiday shopping season, a crucial period for Amazon’s retail business, as consumers contend with elevated living costs and higher fuel prices.Advertising business misses expectationsAmazon’s advertising division also disappointed investors. Revenue rose 12 per cent to $19.6 billion, falling short of analysts’ expectations for growth of 18%. It was the first time in seven quarters that the business missed estimates, according to Reuters.The slowdown contrasted with growth of 26% in the previous quarter and 22% in the year-ago period. Jassy attributed some of the weakness to the timing of the company’s Prime Day shopping event, which took place in the second quarter this year in most major markets, including the US.Amazon said the shift in Prime Day’s timing also affected its overall third-quarter sales growth. Excluding the calendar change, year-on-year revenue growth would have been approximately four percentage points higher, the company said.AI spending pressures spread across Big TechAmazon’s results come amid growing investor scrutiny of the enormous sums technology companies are committing to AI infrastructure and whether the spending will deliver adequate returns.Alphabet, the parent company of Google and YouTube, saw its shares plunge 12% on Thursday after investors reacted to its latest results and rising expenditure on property and equipment. Microsoft, meanwhile, lowered its capital expenditure outlook to $170 billion from $175 billion.The sell-off reflects concerns that the race to build data centres and deploy AI chips could strain cash flows even at some of the industry’s largest companies.Amazon is also facing scrutiny over the impact of its expanding data centre footprint on local communities. Earlier this month, the company said it would invest more than $1 billion over five years in communities where it operates data centres, including funding for education, job training, water conservation and energy-related initiatives.Despite the concerns, Amazon continues to expand its retail operations through faster deliveries, automation and AI-powered warehouse technology. articles.title: Traders' tools stolen every 20 minutes in UK
articles.summary: Gangs and "chancers" are behind the crimes, says an MP calling on the government to do more to help.
articles.body:
Traders' tools worth thousands of pounds were stolen somewhere in the UK every 20 minutes last year, figures show.

At least 26,164 tool thefts were recorded in 2025, based on responses from 30 police forces who shared data. The true figure is likely to be higher as a further 15 forces could not respond.

Gangs and "chancers" are behind the crimes, according to Labour MP Amanda Martin, who is calling for her government to do more to help.

The Home Office said it was "working with the police to tackle and prevent tool theft to protect more hardworking tradespeople", including increasing neighbourhood policing, investing in police and working with industry and AI to tackle the sale of stolen goods.

Lulzim Pjetri owns Alliance Refrigeration Group, a commercial refrigeration business in Aston, Birmingham, from which tools were stolen six times in a year.

On one occasion, thieves broke into a parked van while two staff sat in its cab eating their lunch.

Those responsible were not wearing masks, held up crowbars and told the workers it was not worth them trying to stop it, Pjetri said.

Pjetri said: "Unless they choke the second-hand tool market, this problem will always be there."

"I'm concerned for my guys' safety," said Pjetri, who employs seven people.

"It is our living. It is the emotional trauma that you get from it. It's happening again and again and again and no one out there can see this."

Replacing the tools stolen from each van can cost Pjetri up to £7,000, with a further £4000-£5000 for repairs, and that is before counting the cost of missed work while the vans are off the road - sometimes for weeks at a time.

"You've got to remember these vehicles are supporting the hardest working class of the UK," said Pjetri, who is also known as Mike.

The average value of an insurance claim for tool theft in 2025 was £4,206.60, according to insurers Direct Line for Business.

The biggest cost from multiple tool theft incidents faced by Kerry Field, owner of Change It Homes based in Norton Lindsey, Warwickshire, was £10,000 worth of tools and motorbikes stolen in a break-in.

The BBC has seen CCTV footage showing the thieves making offensive gestures directly at the cameras during the crime.

Field spent a further £10,000 improving security, including new electric gates, cameras and taking on a rescue dog to help keep his headquarters safe.

His staff found one of their stolen saws advertised for sale online, but Field was advised to go to collect it himself when he reported it to police.

The force later apologised and told him the member of staff should not have suggested this, Field said.

"I think it's definitely got worse," he said. "I think a lot of it isn't notified to the police because people know it's not going to make any difference; they're not going to get any tools back.

"It's always been classed as very low level. If you take away someone's livelihood, it has an impact on the whole of society."

He added the lack of consequences for thieves or action by police did not instil confidence, but he understood forces were overstretched.

Warwickshire Police said it took all reports of tool theft "very seriously", but a suspect could not be identified in this case.

A spokesperson added: "Following concerns raised by the victim, the case was re-opened and thoroughly reviewed. No further lines of enquiry were identified."

The Home Office said it had boosted neighbourhood policing, with more than 3,800 additional neighbourhood officers in roles, and was investing "a historic £18.5bn in police force funding".

Martin - whose father was a plumber - has campaigned for tougher sentencing for tool thefts.

"We, as a government, have to do more," said the MP for Portsmouth North.

She said better regulation of the secondhand market was needed, including for pawnbrokers and well-known online retailers and auctioneers.

"It's making sure if you're selling some tools, you've got to have proof that you've owned it," she said.

Businesses with physical stores often require anyone selling goods to provide ID and for transactions to be recorded on CCTV, with other measures including signed undertakings to confirm they can legally sell an item and staff making checks for missing, removed or obscured serial numbers.

Online retailers have published terms and conditions saying they do not accept stolen goods and encourage users to report suspicions if they believe items listed for sale are stolen.

The Home Office said it continued to work with police, industry bodies and online sites to look at the issue of unregulated tool sales and what more could be done.

A common complaint among traders at a conference organised by Fix Radio in Birmingham last week was that when they made insurance claims for stolen tools, the amount repaid would not cover buying new replacements or the business missed out on while waiting for repairs.

Gareth Powley, a senior technical underwriter at Aviva and Direct Line for Business insurance, said it had a "new for old" basis policy.

He said: "The worst thing you want when you have to claim is to be trying to find secondhand tools or to have that shortfall. It's really important to look at the underlying cover you're buying.

"Maybe a cheap policy isn't as good as one providing more full cover."

Businesses can also add a liquid DNA watermark to their tools - which is not clear to the naked eye but glows brightly under UV light - to help trace them and prove their ownership if they are stolen.

Sgt Dave Catlow from the National Business Crime Centre is overseeing a clampdown on tool theft and said organised crime groups were responsible for a large proportion.

Stolen tools were being moved around the UK for resale, as well as abroad, he said.

A five-strong rural gang was jailed last month after a Lincolnshire Police investigation revealed the men frequently used older 4x4 vehicles fitted with cloned registration plates and typically travelled at night, wearing gloves, heavy clothing and face coverings in a bid to conceal their identities.

The Metropolitan Police has now begun to issue notices to car boot sale organisers, warning they could face criminal liability if they knowingly facilitate or ignore the sale of stolen, counterfeit and illicit goods. The warnings are made under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.

Catlow believes this has led to a reduction in stalls selling tools at car boot sales that police have since revisited.

His role is to make sure best practice is shared across different police forces to avoid "displacement" - when one force has success driving down one type of crime locally but culprits move elsewhere.

Bonzer Car Boot Sale in Romford, east London, was visited by The Met earlier this month as part of its operations to deter the resale of stolen tools.

Sniffer dog Kaiser, a two-year-old Alsatian rescue from the company SelectaDNA, joined officers for the operation. He is trained to detect forensic marking or liquid DNA on tools.

The owner of the land where Bonzer Car Boot Sale is held, who did not wish to be named, said: "We don't want to be on the wrong side of the law.

"We don't want individuals who have their power tools stolen not being able to go to work on top of losing the value of those power tools, so we will do whatever we need, whatever we're advised to do, to cut that out."

articles.title: How Israel choked off Hebron at 10 entrances, as 5,000 forced to flee
articles.summary: Our analysis exposes the heavy humanitarian and economic toll of the military siege suffocating Palestinians in Hebron.
articles.body:
Almost 5,000 people have been displaced as a result of Israel’s military siege on the southern West Bank city of Hebron, Al Jazeera reveals.

As the lockdown, which has choked the city off at 10 identified entry points, enters its second week on Friday, the number of people forcibly removed from their homes stands at 4,969. The displaced population includes vulnerable groups: 441 elderly people, 336 infants less than two years old and 312 patients with chronic diseases. More than 200 pregnant or nursing women are also included, as well as 44 people with disabilities.

Al Jazeera, which has analysed municipal data and statistics from human rights groups, reveals that 780 families are currently displaced, representing about 2 percent of the city’s 250,000 residents.

“Thousands of citizens were forced out of their homes, and the world watched children crying after midnight,” Hebron Mayor Yousef al-Jabari told Al Jazeera. He added in a statement to Anadolu agency that Hebron is “facing a severe, massive siege and collective punishment”.

On October 24, the mayor told Al Jazeera that about 2,200 people were displaced, meaning the number had more than doubled in just two days.

The military siege began on Friday, October 23, after two Palestinians shot two Israeli soldiers dead in Hebron and injured three others, before the army killed the two attackers.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced on social media that he had ordered security forces to immediately close Hebron and “prepare for a full lockdown across all of Judea and Samaria [the Israeli term for the occupied West Bank]”.

“We will act to destroy this place, to change it completely,” he proclaimed.

The Israeli army said the operation aims to “thwart terrorism” by searching, arresting suspects, and confiscating weapons.

Defence Minister Israel Katz said Palestinians will not be allowed to return to their homes until Hamas’s “infrastructure” is dismantled.

However, the Israeli news site Ynet quoted the army as saying the search for weapons has had “limited accomplishments” and keeping residents away from their homes for a prolonged period faces “legal difficulties”.

The municipality noted that the targeted eviction zone spans 0.35 square kilometres (0.14 square miles) – the size of 49 football pitches and an area housing more than 500 families comprising at least 2,500 individuals.

Conditions remain precarious; among the families whose locations have been tracked, 283 are residing with relatives and 266 are in locations classified by the municipality as unsafe.

According to Al Jazeera’s findings, most displaced families have sought refuge with relatives or host families in nearby neighbourhoods such as Issa, and no one has resorted to official shelter centres, while only 23 families managed to secure rented homes.

Al Jazeera’s analysis shows that Israeli forces have surrounded the city by closing off 10 entrances located between 2.4km (1.5 miles) and 7.6km (4.7 miles) from the centre.

These blockades include Halhul, Nabi Yunus and Ras al-Jora to the north; Beit Einun to the northeast; and Bir al-Mahjar to the northwest. The eastern and southern flanks are blockaded by closures at Jabal Juhar, al-Fahs, Qalqas, al-Harayiq and Dura.

The closed military operations zone lies about 2km (1.2 miles) west of the city centre, covering a documented area of at least 0.29sq km (0.11sq miles), or about 40 football fields.

In the Farsh al-Hawa area at the city’s western entrance, Israeli forces demolished a three-apartment residential building during the first two days of the operation – October 23 and 24 – targeted a ceramics company alongside car parts shops, and bulldozed approximately 7,000 square metres (75,000 square feet) of land.

Families were also evicted from the al-Jalda and Ein Deir Bahha neighbourhoods about midnight on Friday, October 23, when Israeli forces ordered residents via loudspeakers to leave.

During the first two days of the operation, forces converted several homes into military barracks and raised Israeli flags on them, according to Anadolu.

Over the first six days of the operation, the Israeli military arrested approximately 110 Palestinians across the governorate, according to the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society (PPS).

The detainees include seven children, people with special needs, and dozens of former prisoners. Israeli forces also arrested three women, releasing two while keeping the third under interrogation at the al-Mascobiyeh detention centre.

Furthermore, the military continues to hold eight relatives of the two Palestinian gunmen who killed the Israeli soldiers, having transferred them to interrogation centres.

Beyond formal arrests, hundreds of citizens have been subjected to field interrogations during military raids.

The PPS reported that these interrogations, conducted on streets, at checkpoints and inside homes, have been accompanied by severe beatings and abuse.

The military has searched more than 500 sites in the city.

The Israeli army claims to have discovered a 15-metre- (50ft-) deep underground pit containing an electronic device near an attacker’s home, although the property owner has denied this. The owner said the excavation is a sewage cesspit for an area lacking infrastructure, adding that the property belongs to neither of the gunmen and is more than 100 metres (330ft) from their residences.

The Hebron Chamber of Commerce and Industry estimates daily commercial losses at 12 million shekels (about $3.8m) as a result of this siege.

Factory production capacity has plummeted by 40 to 60 percent, according to estimates by Adnan al-Natsheh, vice president of the Chamber.

The governorate houses about 3,500 industrial facilities, in particular plastics and dairy facilities, as well as 70 percent of the gold workshops for the Palestinian market.

The movement of commercial trucks has completely halted. The demolitions in Farsh al-Hawa alone have caused damage of more than two million shekels (about $640,000).

This recent escalation compounds an already heavy toll across the occupied West Bank.

In September alone, the Hebron governorate faced 272 attacks, including 122 perpetrated by Israeli settlers, and 19 demolition operations that levelled 91 structures, making it the most targeted governorate in the West Bank for demolitions.

articles.title: Precio de la luz por horas hoy, viernes 30 de octubre: cuándo es más barata y más cara en el día
articles.standfirst: El precio de la luz se encarece 5.92 euros este viernes
articles.summary: El precio de la luz se encarece 5.92 euros este viernes
articles.body: Hoy, el precio medio de la electricidad se sitúa en 244,69 €/MWh, lo que representa un incremento de 13,68 € respecto al día anterior, que fue de 231,01 €/MWh. Al ser viernes, muchos consumidores se preparan para el fin de semana. Analizaremos a continuación cuáles son las horas más caras y más baratas para optimizar el consumo eléctrico. Los precios de la luz tienden a ser más altos durante las horas pico de consumo energético, especialmente en la franja de la tarde y la noche. Se observa un bloque continuo de horas caras desde las 18:00 a 20:00, donde los precios alcanzan los 316.94 €/MWh y 312.90 €/MWh, respectivamente. Además, otro tramo significativo se encuentra entre las 07:00 y 09:00, con precios que van desde 290.88 €/MWh a 292.06 €/MWh. Estos valores indican que el consumo elevado en las horas clave provoca un aumento notable en las tarifas. La electricidad es más barata durante las primeras horas de la madrugada y a primera hora del día. Las mejores oportunidades de ahorro se concentran entre las 02:00 - 03:00 (233.74 €/MWh), 03:00 - 04:00 (231.12 €/MWh) y 04:00 - 05:00 (227.81 €/MWh), donde se observa un claro descenso en los precios. Además, entre las 10:00 - 11:00 (227.96 €/MWh) y 12:00 - 13:00 (174.12 €/MWh) también existen tramos con valores significativamente bajos, ofreciendo una ventana amplia de precios asequibles y múltiples oportunidades reales de ahorro. En el análisis de la jornada, destaca una amplia diferencia de precios, que alcanza su punto máximo con un salto considerable entre las franjas horarias de la tarde y la noche, lo que resalta la volatilidad de la tarifa a lo largo del día. Este patrón es crucial para los consumidores, ya que sugiere que gestionar el consumo en las horas adecuadas puede suponer un ahorro significativo en la factura.

articles.title: Oil flows are up as Iran war turmoil eases. Why do prices keep rising?
articles.summary: Brent crude prices are up more than 60 percent compared with pre-war levels, despite rebound in supply.
articles.body:
Oil flows out of the Gulf have increased substantially, easing the huge supply disruption caused by the United States/Israel war on Iran.

Crude exports from the Gulf averaged 24.6 million barrels per day (bpd) in the week to October 18, exceeding the pre-war average, according to market intelligence firm Kpler.

Brent crude, the global benchmark, is trading at its highest prices since April, up more than 60 percent compared with before the war.

On Friday, Brent crude front-month futures – contracts for oil deliveries in December – rose more than 2 percent to briefly top $117 a barrel.

The climbing prices reflect anxiety about the possibility of renewed hostilities in the US war on Iran, dwindling oil stocks , and the increased costs of transporting supplies out of the region, according to market analysts.

“The market is doing exactly what it is supposed to do: It is telling us there is plenty of prompt oil, but there is no end to this war in sight – in fact … escalation is very likely,” Adi Imsirovic, a lecturer in energy systems at the University of Oxford, told Al Jazeera.

“Therefore, futures markets reflect that expectation,” Imsirovic, a veteran oil trader, said.

Oil producers have become increasingly adept at responding to the volatile climate in the Middle East to keep supplies flowing.

Facing the threat of Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, shipping lines have established a shuttle system involving ship-to-ship transfers off Oman and the United Arab Emirates to reduce the distance any one vessel must travel in perilous waters.

Shuttle boats carry the oil through the strait and load it onto waiting tankers once they are out of the danger zone.

In August, more than 70 percent of the crude that crossed the strait did so via ship-to-ship transfers, according to Kpler.

Oil producers have also ramped up exports that bypass the strait altogether via Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline , which carries oil supplies from its eastern oil fields to its Yanbu port on the Red Sea in the west, and the United Arab Emirates’ Habshan-Fujairah pipeline.

As of September, 40 percent of exports from the Gulf were bypassing the strait, a conduit for one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies during peacetime, compared with 17 percent before the war, according to Kpler data.

Such workarounds have nonetheless come at a cost.

Freight costs have reached as much as $40 per barrel in recent weeks, about 10 times the usual rate, according to data from the London Stock Exchange Group, the surge driven by elevated insurance premiums in addition to logistical challenges.

October has been the deadliest month for attacks on commercial vessels since the start of the war, with 32 incidents logged by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) as of Friday.

“So barrels are moving, but neither smoothly nor reliably. That should not be read as a sign of normalisation,” Isabel Figuerola-Ferretti, an expert in oil markets at Comillas Pontifical University in Madrid, Spain, told Al Jazeera.

“Delivering a barrel has become far more expensive,” Figuerola-Ferretti said.

While market intelligence data has shown exports reaching pre-war levels at various points in recent weeks, the longer-term supply trend is less clear.

Pavel Molchanov, an investment strategist at Raymond James & Associates, expressed scepticism that supply has returned to the pre-conflict trend.

“The IEA’s most recent production data – for September – shows OPEC Gulf production at 15.8 million bpd, which equates to 75 percent of the pre-war baseline,” Molchanov told Al Jazeera, referring to the International Energy Agency’s latest energy outlook.

“That slightly surpassed July’s 74 percent to reach the highest level since the start of the war, but it’s still a considerable distance from 100 percent.”

Meanwhile, oil stockpiles, a buffer during supply disruptions, are waning.

Observed inventories fell by 10 million barrels in September, taking the global stockpile to 509 million barrels below its pre-war level, according to the IEA.

“The market has moved to a chronic squeeze, driven by concrete supply risks: Hormuz transit, shipping and depleted inventories,” Figuerola-Ferretti said.

With no permanent end to the Iran war in sight, few analysts see prices returning to normal anytime soon.

Brent futures for delivery in October 2027 stood at more than $90 a barrel on Friday, in a sign that markets see normality as a long way off, still.

“When could prices return to $70? Not soon,” Figuerola-Ferretti said.

“It would need durable de-escalation, a return to normal transit and shipping conditions through Hormuz, rebuilt inventories and freight costs back to normal,” she added.

Molchanov, the investment strategist, said he did not believe supply could realistically exceed 85 percent of pre-war levels without a permanent diplomatic solution to the war.

“Once the political groundwork is in place, the next steps will be logistical: Demining Hormuz, bringing shipping crews back to work, and resuming production at currently shut-in oilfields,” he said.

articles.title: Canada’s economic break with the US in 5 charts
articles.summary: For decades, the United States and Canada worked to build one of the world’s closest economic partnerships, with supply chains, businesses and trade increasingly intertwined.
articles.body: For decades, the United States and Canada worked to build one of the world’s closest economic partnerships, with supply chains, businesses and trade increasingly intertwined. But now, with the two countries in the thick of a trade war, Canada is taking a dramatic step to reduce its reliance on the United States. It is forging closer economic ties with the European Union and is set to become its first-ever “associate member.” “Economic integration is now being weaponized, and tariffs are being used as a means of pressure,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told EU lawmakers last month in a parliamentary address. Carney was referring to President Donald Trump’s ramped-up trade war with Canada. Over the summer Trump levied 50% tariffs on around $20 billion worth of Canadian goods and, in some cases, imposing outright import bans. Canada matched those duties and has vowed to match any future tariffs. Forthcoming data is likely to show trade between the two nations fell as a result. It’s uncertain how the EU-Canada partnership could look and whether it will even come to fruition at all, as officials from Germany and France, key EU member states, have voiced opposition. Carney has also been met with backlash from Canadian officials who feel it compromises Canada’s sovereignty. That hasn’t stopped Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. On Thursday they invited other countries to join in the initiative they dubbed “Alliance for the Future.” “In a world of growing rivalries, sovereignty and independence are no longer just the freedom to act alone — it is the capacity to act together,” von der Leyen said in an address Thursday at this week’s two-day Canada-EU summit in Montreal. “And this is why we will build an alliance for the future,” she said. “And we start with Canada.” Few details have been shared about what Canada’s association membership with the EU could look like, though Carney said earlier this week he intends to use the summit as an opportunity to further nail down the next steps. And while trade ruptures with the US were the impetus for Carney’s push with the EU, the impact of the trade war with the US has not been limited to trade. From vacations to investments, here’s how the fallout is showing up across both economies. A trend of declining trade While Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods and Carney’s retaliatory measures against American goods over the summer likely weighed on trade, they’d represent just the latest chapter in a broader decline in trade between the two countries. The total value of trade between the US and Canada has fallen since 2022. Of those three years, the largest annual drop came last year, when Trump imposed 50% tariffs on steel and aluminum, two of the top goods the US imports from Canada. Canada is sending the smallest share of its exports to the US in nearly 30 years Most of Canada’s exports — historically between 70% and 80% — go to the US. While the US remains Canada’s largest export market by far, its share of Canadian exports has fallen sharply since Trump returned to office, reflecting heightened trade uncertainty, according to a report published last year by Global Affairs Canada’s Office of the Chief Economist. Over this period, Canada significantly increased its exports to Europe and Central Asia as it looked to wean itself off its reliance on the US market. Carney, in a statement Thursday unveiling an initiative titled “The Plan for a Stronger Canada,” said that the shift is intended “to create greater security and prosperity for Canadians.” In addition to trade, the effort is aimed at strengthening national defense and boosting public safety. Alcohol became an early casualty Alcohol accounts for a relatively small share of trade between the two countries, but it has become one of the most visible symbols of their deteriorating economic relationship. In March 2025, provincial liquor boards across Canada pulled American products from their shelves. Customers visiting the government-run liquor stores were met with empty shelves and “BUY CANADIAN INSTEAD” signs. The fallout showed up immediately in trade data, with US alcohol exports to Canada plunging and remaining well below previous levels. American spirits were hit particularly hard. Exports to Canada fell to a record low of $9.7 million in the second quarter of 2025 before rebounding to more than $20 million in each of the third and fourth quarters, according to the Distilled Spirits Council. The retaliation has since gone both ways. Last month, Trump imposed a ban on most Canadian liquor shipped to the US. Canadians are spending less time — and money — in the US Trump has repeatedly floated the idea of making Canada the 51st state, drawing the ire of many Canadians. He further inflamed tensions recently by renaming Lake Ontario “Lake Canada.” Canadians’ disdain for Trump has been apparent in travel data. Canadian visits to the US peaked at nearly 80 million in the early 1990s before settling at around 40 million a year in subsequent decades. In 2025, visits to the US fell to 29.1 million — the lowest level outside the pandemic era since records began in 1972, according to Statistics Canada. The decline is taking a bite out of US businesses. Canadians spent $16.1 billion in the US in 2024, according to Statistics Canada, but that fell to $13.4 billion in 2025, a $2.7 billion drop in a single year. Canadian investors staged a record retreat from US stocks After pouring $78.1 billion CAD (around $56 billion USD) into US stocks in the first half of 2026, Canadian investors abruptly reversed course in July, selling a record $31 billion CAD (around $22 billion USD) according to Statistics Canada. The sell-off was concentrated in shares of large US technology companies. It came as the S&P 500 edged lower in July after strong gains earlier in the year.

articles.title: Amazon, Alphabet, SpaceX and Meta are all to blame for the new tech stock rout
articles.summary: The tech stock rout only has one driving factor behind it.
articles.body:
Don't blame Intel's ( INTC ) weak guidance, tied to a prolonged memory chip supply shortage , for the fresh rout on tech stocks.

Blame the hyperscalers like Amazon ( AMZN ), Alphabet ( GOOGL ) and Meta ( META ) for not guiding Wall Street properly on how much they intended to spend this year and next on AI infrastructure. The bills are coming in much larger than expected, and Wall Street can't stomach it.

That's why you aren't seeing many heroes out there saying buy the dip right now. That's why Friday is shaping up to be another bloodbath for tech stocks.

Remember, it's cash flow that will be used to repay all the debt hyperscalers are poised to incur to support their robust AI infrastructure buildouts. The fact that cash flow is drying up because of a protracted period of spending is the bug causing the debt and stock markets to catch a cold.

Kudos to Amazon for at least not burying its free cash flow metric, the most important metric for tech at the moment, at the bottom of its earnings release. It made it no less tough to stomach, but at least it was easy to find quickly.

Amazon's free cash flow decreased to an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing twelve months, driven primarily by a year-over-year increase of $94.8 billion in purchases of property and equipment. This increase primarily reflects investments in artificial intelligence, Amazon said.

This compares to a free cash flow inflow of $14.8 billion for the trailing twelve months ended Sept. 30 of last year.

"We still expect 2026 cash capex of approximately $220 billion, the majority for AWS, and expect to spend meaningfully more in 2027," Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on his earnings call.

Amazon's stock is down 7% in pre-market trading today.

On Wednesday evening, Google posted negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the quarter versus a Wall Street estimate for negative $3.5 billion.

Thursday saw more than $500 billion in market value wiped off Google.

Meta dropped a bombshell in its third quarter results last week, posting negative free cash flow for the first time since 2012. SpaceX ( SPCX ) burned about $9.9 billion in free cash flow in the quarter.

Both stocks have continued to sell off post earnings.

Hyperscaler free cash flow is likely to stay negative points out EvercoreISI strategist Julian Emanuel. The hyperscaler cohort of Meta, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Oracle ( ORCL ) and SpaceX ( SPCX ) is now near a negative $200 billion expected over the next year Emanuel's research shows.

This is what the market is pricing in today. Painful, yes.

articles.title: The Magnificent 7 stocks are seeing stunning declines

Meta and Alphabet are effectively in bear markets, down more than 20% from their 52-week highs, as the Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace graphic shows below. Tesla is off by 19.2%, Amazon by 15.1%, and AI chip darling Nvidia by 12.2%.

Meta, Alphabet, Amazon and Tesla have been crushed following their earnings reports that showed pressured free cash flow amid aggressive AI spending. Nvidia is down because of the fear that all of these hyperscalers are overspending and will be forced to pull back in 2027.

Apple and Microsoft are the only Mag 7 names hanging tough, for company-specific reasons.

Microsoft managed to show positive free cash flow this week alongside strong Azure sales growth. Apple isn't being viewed as an AI play. It's seen more as a cash-rich play rolling out new hardware in the iPhone and Mac realms.

"There is too much weakness in tech for the market to ignore," BTIG strategist Jonathan Krinsky said.

Too much weakness in seven of the most important stocks in the world for the market to ignore is more like it.

articles.title: Are banks cyber-ready? RBI seeks proof of compliance amid rising attacks
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has asked banks to step up their cybersecurity measures and demonstrate compliance with existing rules amid a
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has asked banks to step up their cybersecurity measures and demonstrate compliance with existing rules amid a rise in attacks on financial institutions. According to three people familiar with the matter cited by Reuters, the central bank also asked banks to check their application programming interfaces (APIs) for security gaps. These software links connect banks with non-bank lenders and fintech companies, making them a key area of concern, the sources said.The RBI has also sought information on how banks are preparing for risks associated with artificial intelligence (AI), as hackers increasingly use sophisticated tools to target financial infrastructure globally. Such attacks threaten both customer information and funds.One of the sources, a person aware of regulatory thinking, said hackers consider smaller lenders, non-bank lenders and their third-party service providers to be "softer targets".Although the RBI has already laid down directives for banks to manage cybersecurity risks, their implementation remains inadequate, said a second source, a consultant working with top banks. The regulator is now pressing banks to ensure stronger implementation of these requirements, the person added.Recent cyber incidents put lenders under scrutinyThe concerns come against the backdrop of several cyber incidents reported in India's financial sector in recent weeks.State Bank of India, the country's largest lender, recently reported a data leak involving around 3,900 customers. The bank said last week that it was investigating the incident but had not yet identified the vulnerability responsible.In another incident, two Mumbai-based non-bank lenders suffered losses of around $2 million following more than 700 unauthorised instant transfers from accounts maintained with ICICI Bank on October 8 and 9, Reuters reported.According to the complaint, hackers had compromised the API connection through which loan disbursal instructions were sent to ICICI Bank.The threat has also drawn attention from India's cybersecurity agency CERT-In. In an advisory issued on October 9, the agency warned that hackers were stealing banks' API credentials to move money out of lenders' own systems, potentially with the assistance of AI-based tools.CERT-In also conducted cybersecurity training earlier this week for 300 officials from more than 55 financial institutions, according to a post shared by the agency on its social media handle on X.The RBI's actions come as financial regulators globally are increasing their efforts to address the cybersecurity risks associated with AI. Authorities in the United States and Britain are among those stepping up measures to contain these threats, Reuters reported earlier this month.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Chevron stock rose 1% before the bell on Friday.

He noted that U.S. upstream production exceeded 2 million barrels of oil equivalent per day for the fifth consecutive quarter.

articles.title: Intel and Sandisk have very different views about what's going on in memory chips
articles.summary: Two must-listen earnings calls from two big names in tech. Two very different views on what's going on in memory chips. One outcome for both stocks: Big decl...
articles.body:
Two must-listen earnings calls from two big names in tech. Two very different views on what's going on in memory chips. One outcome for both stocks: Big declines.

Intel ( INTC ) stock is getting torched in premarket trading on Friday, falling 26%, after the company warned of sluggish PC sales in the current quarter. At the core of that warning is consumer resistance to the higher PC prices stemming from the memory chip shortage.

Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan sees more challenging quarters ahead due to memory chip dynamics.

"Our customers began signaling a PC slowdown based on the memory prices and availability," Tan said. "Year-to-date system endpoint prices have increased significantly, placing additional pressure on already limited IT budgets. The pace of this PC correction has accelerated over the last two months as our OEM partners are aggressively managing inventory to match the softer sell-through."

"We expect the current environment to persist until memory availability and prices begin to normalize," Tan added. "While the next few quarters will be challenging for the PC market, our roadmap continues to strengthen, and our long-term outlook remains positive."

On the other hand, hop onto the earnings call late Thursday from memory chipmaker Sandisk ( SNDK ), and you would've heard that there is no memory chip shortage at all. Or, at the very least, things stand to improve nicely in the months ahead.

"We think our internal models are every segment in the NAND market," Sandisk CEO David Goeckeler said. "PCs, smartphones, data center will all show positive growth next year because content per device continues to go up as part of that is mixing to premium."

He added, "So there is no doubt there has been a market adjustment. In many ways, as I said, from a unit basis, we are in the teeth of that on a year-over-year basis, but we see improvement from here."

Sandisk shares are trading down 8% in premarket trading, likely in sympathy with the Intel warning.

So who is right here on memory? The truth lies somewhere in the middle.

But it is clear that a shortage benefits no one, especially Intel and Sandisk shareholders.

articles.title: Reddit shares plunge 23% on DAUs deceleration, weak guidance
articles.summary: Investing.com -- Reddit reported third-quarter results that topped analyst estimates, but shares sank sharply after the social media company issued a weaker-...
articles.body:
Investing.com -- Reddit ( RDDT ) reported third-quarter results that topped analyst estimates, but shares sank sharply after the social media company issued a weaker-than-expected revenue outlook and warned of accelerating declines in search referral traffic.

The stock was down about 23% in premarket trading Friday by 04:39 ET (08:39 GMT).

Reddit reported adjusted earnings of $1.40 per share, beating the consensus estimate of $1.33. Revenue rose 53% year over year to $895 million, above expectations of $874.9 million.

However, the company forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $1.00 billion to $1.03 billion, putting the midpoint of $1.015 billion below Wall Street's $1.05 billion estimate.

The outlook comes as Reddit faces mounting pressure from changes in how users discover content online. Search referral traffic declined meaningfully in the third quarter, with the downturn accelerating toward the end of the period, CEO Steve Huffman said in a shareholder letter.

In October, search traffic fell by more than 1 million referrals per week on average. If the trend continues, Reddit warned that daily active unique users (DAUs) could decline by a low-double-digit percentage in the fourth quarter from its current base of 130.3 million.

Reddit's DAUs grew 12% in the third quarter, a 6 percentage point slowdown from the previous quarter. The shortfall came mainly from U.S. logged-out users as Google's AI Overviews cut referral traffic from one of Reddit's largest user acquisition channels.

"RDDT's delivery of strong Revenue/EBITDA growth (53%/70%) was overshadowed by worsening U.S. DAU declines, as increased prevalence of AI Overview negatively impacted referral traffic," Jefferies analyst John Colantuoni said.

"Growth is also expected to slow in 4Q, which is likely to raise concern about sustainability. We think the stock could be rangebound near-term until a recovery in user trends emerges, but still like the long-term story as monetization upside helps drive peer-leading revenue growth," he added.

Weekly active uniques grew 16% to 515.2 million.

KeyBanc Capital Markets downgraded Reddit after the earnings release. "We are downgrading shares of RDDT from OW to SW as our thesis is not playing out; search traffic is a larger headwind than envisioned (potential for a LDD% q/q decline in 4Q), and this creates more uncertainty around '27E/'28E revenue and EBITDA," they wrote.

articles.title: Big Oil is raking in huge profits. Shareholders like Trump are cashing in. You’re paying for it with high gas prices.
articles.summary: Big Oil minted money as the Iran war delivered American drivers the highest gas prices on record for the third quarter.
articles.body: Big Oil minted big money as the Iran war delivered American drivers the highest gas prices on record for the third quarter. The two biggest US oil companies posted huge jumps in profit on Friday. ExxonMobil earned $15.4 billion in the third quarter, slightly more than doubled from what it earned a year ago, while Chevron’s adjusted earnings were up 186%, to $10.4 billion. Analysts forecast both could report record profits for the full year. Global oil prices are spiking as the US-Iran war drags on, leading to blockbuster profits for oil companies and higher gas prices for US drivers. The national average for gasoline during the third quarter was $4.12 a gallon, according to AAA, up 96 cents from a year ago and the highest on record for the quarter. High gas prices are a headache for the Trump administration as the midterm election approaches. Many voters are angry about what they pay at the pump. Farmers are also struggling to afford diesel fuel to run their equipment during harvest, and some homeowners are paying record heating oil costs. US households have now paid $1,184 more on average since the start of the war, thanks to more expensive gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, according to Moody’s Analytics. But last week, President Donald Trump said high profits for the oil industry was a good thing for Americans. “Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what’s happened in the Middle East, because they’re coming to Texas and they’re coming to Oklahoma and they’re coming to Louisiana and they’re taking that oil,” he said at a campaign event in Georgia on Saturday. “We’re making a freaking fortune.” The White House defended the comments to CNN. “The President is pointing to the United States’ position as the world’s top producer and exporter of oil,” a White House official told CNN. “By unleashing American energy dominance, he has strengthened our national security and made our country wealthier.” It’s not just American oil companies cashing in on high oil prices. London-based Shell Oil Thursday reported profit of $12 billion in the third quarter, up 127% from a year earlier. One group that is definitely getting wealthier is those invested in oil companies, including Trump himself. ExxonMobil and Chevron shares have both risen 52% so far this year through Thursday’s close, and both rose about more than 1% in premarket trading Friday on the earnings reports. Democrats on Congress’ Joint Economic Committee last weekend found that, based upon Trump’s financial disclosure documents, his ownership in these companies grew by as much as $35.8 million in the first half of this year, which brings his net oil and gas holdings to as much as $81.6 million. The Democrats also found that 94% of Trump’s 2026 oil and gas purchases occurred after the start of the war. The White House said there was nothing improper about the returns that Trump made on oil stocks this year, and said the gains reflected the positive stock market performance under his administration that has delivered “real gains for American companies and hardworking families.” “Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold,” said White House spokesman Davis Ingle. “All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers. There are no conflicts of interest.”

articles.title: North Korean hackers linked to record-breaking $6.3 billion Binance crypto heist
articles.summary: Bitcoin tumbled on Thursday after Binance announced a 'potential security issue' and froze $3 billion in crypto assets.
articles.body:
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, was hit late Thursday by what investigators are say is the biggest crypto hack in history. with $6.3 billion in digital assets affected.

Binance has temporarily suspended customer withdrawals. The company and outside investigators are racing to track down the stolen funds. It said in a X post that $3 billion of the total estimated $6.3 billion in affected assets have been "frozen on-chain so far." Customer withdrawals should resume by Sunday, Binance CEO Yi He said in a separate social media post.

Binance added it "will cover all losses" from using its Secure Asset Fund for users and company reserves.

"User funds are safe," the exchange said, adding that it temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks are completed.

The Thursday attack has rattled crypto markets and related stocks. Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) prices tumbled to around $77,000 on Thursday night.

Other major crypto assets also tumbled on following the hack, led by Ether ( ETH-USD ), which dropped 4% to around $2,200. Binance's native token, BNB ( BND-USD ), also plunged by more than 5%.

Crypto-related stocks were set to open lower on Friday. Shares of Circle, trading platforms Coinbase ( COIN ) and Robinhood ( HOOD ) and digital-asset Treasury giant Strategy ( MSTR ) tumbled more than 6% in Friday's premarket.

The frozen assets appear to include over $2 billion stablecoins, which have been frozen. Tether, the world's largest stablecoin issuer, "froze more than 1.567B" of its USDT stablecoin in relation to the hack," CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X . The second largest issuer, Circle ( CRCL ), froze another $800 million "in coordination with law enforcement," CEO Jeremy Allaire said.

Although full details aren't yet available, the hack is shaping up to be the largest crypto theft in history, far exceeding the previous record set in February 2025 when attackers nabbed $1.5 billion from crypto derivatives exchange ByBit.

Blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Elliptic have linked the theft to North Korean hackers, with TRM attributing the theft "with high confidence" to the same group responsible for last year's Bybit hack, known as TraderTraitor.

Elliptic estimated Friday that about 44% of the stolen assets have been frozen, with stablecoins accounting nearly all of those funds. The firm estimated that attackers still controlled over $3 billion in crypto that cannot be directly frozen by token issuers.

The hackers appear to have compromised Binance's wallet-signing infrastructure, allowing them to authorize transactions that drained billions of dollars in cryptocurrency across multiple blockchains, according to the firms. Binance at its preliminary stage, its investigation into the hack suggests an engineer's laptop was compromised. The exchange added that it has found no evidence wallet passwords were leaked

articles.title: Intel plunges as much as 26%, briefly on pace for its worst day since 1974
articles.summary: A weak outlook has Intel on pace for one of its worst days in half a century.
articles.body:
Intel's data center business just grew almost 80% in a year. Its outlook for the fourth quarter is sending the stock toward one of its worst days in half a century, erasing more than $100 billion in market value Friday.

Intel ( INTC ) stock fell as much as 26% Friday after the chipmaker's forecast for the final three months of the year came in well short of Wall Street's expectations.

Only two days in Intel's history were worse, according to Yahoo Finance calculations from Norgate Data closing prices going back to May 1973. The stock fell nearly 30% on July 5, 1974, and about 26% on Aug. 2, 2024.

A close below about $68 would top the 2024 drop and make Friday the worst day since 1974. Below about $64.50, it would be the worst on record.

The sell-off caps a wild year. Intel stock nearly quadrupled from the start of 2026 to its June 22 record. Even after Friday's drop, it's still up more than 80% this year, but it has given back about half its value since that peak.

It has also broken below the $80 zone that held at its July low, and it's on track for its lowest close since April 23. The next day, Intel had its best day since at least 1973, a gain of about 24%.

The quarter itself was strong. Intel topped estimates with adjusted earnings per share of $0.52, and data center revenue jumped to $7.3 billion.

The outlook is what broke the stock. Intel expects fourth quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, below the roughly $17 billion analysts expected, and earnings per share of $0.25 against forecasts of $0.43.

The PC market is the problem . AI data centers are soaking up the world's memory chips, pushing up prices for laptops and desktops. Intel now expects PC shipments to fall about 12% this year and another 10% in 2027. An accident at its Israel factory will cost about $300 million in fourth quarter revenue on top of that.

Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon called the outlook "(in a word) terrible" and cut his price target to $75 from $110.

PC makers Dell ( DELL ) and HP ( HPQ ) slid too, adding to a tech stock rout that has hit Alphabet ( GOOGL , GOOG ) and Amazon ( AMZN ) after their reports this week.

Intel said the PC slump won't let up until memory supply and prices return to normal.

"Rebuilding Intel is going to be a multiyear journey, and I remain firmly committed to making it happen," CEO Lip-Bu Tan said on Thursday's earnings call.

articles.title: AstraZeneca profit jumps 23% on cancer drugs as it unveils major savings plan
articles.summary: AstraZeneca's net profit jumped 23% in the third quarter on booming sales of its cancer drugs, as the British drugmaker unveiled a programme to save $1.5 bil...
articles.body:
AstraZeneca ( AZN ), Britain's biggest pharmaceutical company, said on Friday that its profit after tax rose 23% to $3.12 billion (€2.79bn) for the July to September period, driven largely by its cancer treatments.

That marks a sharp pick-up from the rise of just over 2% in the previous quarter. The firm also launched a plan to generate $1.5 billion (€1.34bn) in annual savings, which it intends to reinvest mainly in the drugs it has in development.

Revenue grew 7% to $16.2 billion (€14.5bn).

Oncology, its biggest business, accounted for 48% of the total, with sales up 17% to $7.8 billion (€6.99bn), led by lung cancer drug Tagrisso and immunotherapy Imfinzi. Core earnings per share, which exclude items such as restructuring costs and the amortisation of acquired drugs, rose 17% to $2.79.

The savings drive, called Reshaping for Sustainable Growth, will cost up to $2 billion (€1.79bn) in one-off restructuring charges and is due to be largely complete by the end of 2029.

AstraZeneca said the savings would be reinvested in the company, principally in its pipeline of new drugs, as it plans to "redeploy resources" across its existing business to back more than 180 projects in development.

Such restructuring could mean job cuts, though none have been announced.

"With multiple potential blockbuster assets in late-stage development and transformative technologies scaling rapidly, we are on track to deliver our 2030 ambition," CEO Pascal Soriot said in a statement.

The growth came despite pressure on older medicines.

Sales of Farxiga, its treatment for diabetes, heart and kidney disease, fell 25% to $1.6 billion (€1.43bn) after cheaper generic versions hit the US market, while blood thinner Brilinta also lost patent protection.

AstraZeneca is also facing volume-based procurement in China, a state bulk-buying scheme that forces drugmakers to cut prices in exchange for large orders.

The company confirmed its outlook for 2026, expecting revenue to grow by a mid-to-high single-digit percentage and core earnings per share by a low double-digit percentage, excluding currency swings.

It remains on track for its target of $80 billion (€71.7bn) in annual revenue by 2030, compared with almost $59 billion (€52.9bn) in 2025, and expects half of that to come from the US.

The company has been leaning further into the American market, adding a direct share listing in New York in February, while also pledging to invest $15 billion (€13.4bn) in China by 2030.

It has reported 12 positive results from late-stage trials so far this year, and is also developing a weight-loss treatment to compete with drugs such as Novo Nordisk's Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Mounjaro.

AstraZeneca shares were up over 4.5% in early trading on Friday.
